leading_positions.synthesis: Mattson and Sem-Sandberg each prefer Mircea Cărtărescu in their round 1 configurations. They rest the case on a recognizable, densely patterned Romanian prose voice and on an architecture of memory, body and dream that extends across volumes (Blinding; Solenoid). Both would anchor the citation in the prose project, with poetry as foundation rather than a co-equal claim. Both state that they cannot settle from the evidence whether the later volumes deepen or repeat their motifs, and that translation may flatten the sentence-level Romanian. The files do not show agreement on how much poetry and essay coverage should count. Cărtărescu is named as a first choice or alternative in all six files, but that is not a statement of preference for him as laureate.

Carlberg and Palm each prefer Anne Carson. They cite an unmistakable voice, formal renewal across lyric, verse novel, essay and translation, and a tie between formal invention and emotional and intellectual substance (Autobiography of Red; Nox). Both say the citation must not rest on the novelty of hybridity alone, and both name Cărtărescu as a strong alternative. Their proposed citations differ: Carlberg centres the encounter between ancient and modern writing, while Palm also names translation and the book as object. Neither can fully judge design-dependent works in translation. Olsson and Sem-Sandberg list Carson as an alternative; Sward lists her as an alternative; Mattson, who ranks her fifth, says her case is substantial and her ranking may understate it.

Sward alone prefers Yoko Tawada. The case is that bilingual writing in Japanese and German makes linguistic estrangement a formal method across fiction, poetry, essays and drama, not a single-book reputation (The Emissary; Memoirs of a Polar Bear). Sward, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Carlberg all note that translation coverage of the German-language and Japanese-language corpora is uneven and that the poetry and drama are least visible. Sem-Sandberg raises a concern that some shorter works may feel slight against their premise. Carlberg and Palm list B001 as an alternative, as does Mattson, who names Tawada as her main alternative.

I alone prefer Adonis. The case is a remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and sustained argument with inherited forms (Songs of Mihyar the Damascene; A Time Between Ashes and Roses), with the critical essays treated as part of that project. I state that my judgment depends on translation, that I cannot show the later collections sustain the earlier level, and that historical influence must be separated from the continuing force of the poems. Sem-Sandberg lists Adonis as an alternative and ranks him second. Mattson ranks him fourth and Carlberg and Sward sixth. Palm ranks him seventh. The ranking differences are attributed in the files to limits in assessing Arabic prosody, not to a dismissal of his importance.

areas_of_agreement: All six files give a preferred configuration of exactly one writer and one prize part. No file proposes a multiwriter configuration, an organization or a translator. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg share B029, and Carlberg and Palm share B012. No ballot has more than two explicit first-choice supporters, and no configuration reaches the four-vote majority.

All six members state that they have not independently verified or re-read the works and that their judgments rest on public knowledge. All six say translation limits what they can assess: Arabic prosody (Adonis), the rhythmic Romanian sentence (Cărtărescu), typography and physical design (Carson), and wordplay across Japanese and German (Tawada).

Members who discuss fame, historical influence, age, readership and political or public positions say these are not literary merit and should not decide the matter for or against a candidate. This is explicit for Adonis in my file and in those of Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Carlberg.

Several members say a citation should rest on a core of the strongest books or the sustained method, not on peripheral works or on novelty of form alone. Palm and Carlberg say this for Carson, Mattson and Sem-Sandberg for Cărtărescu, and Sward for Tawada.

Cărtărescu is named as a first choice or alternative in all six files, and Carson in five of six. Tawada is named in four of six and Adonis in two of six. These counts describe only explicit first choices and listed alternatives. They are not a ranking of merit or a forecast of any vote.
scientific_disputes: Large-scale architecture versus formal variety. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg weigh Cărtărescu's cumulative scale and sustained project most heavily. Sward weighs Tawada's method across genres and two languages above scale. Carlberg and Palm weigh Carson's formal renewal across genres, with Palm conceding that Cărtărescu fits a standard of large-scale sustained architecture more naturally.

Depth or excess in Cărtărescu. Mattson, Sem-Sandberg, Palm and Carlberg raise whether the density and encyclopedic self-reflexive mode deepen across the largest novels or repeat motifs. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg leave it open pending close reading of the later volumes.

Carson as lasting literature or learned game. Mattson asks this explicitly. Carlberg and Palm answer that the apparatus serves grief and desire in Nox and Autobiography of Red. Sem-Sandberg doubts consistency across many experimental and performance-oriented projects. Palm and Carlberg answer by separating core books from peripheral pieces.

Comparing short, hybrid or design-dependent corpora with large novelistic or poetic oeuvres under common criteria. Mattson, Palm, Carlberg, Sem-Sandberg and Olsson raise this. Palm argues the will does not require a large-architecture standard, and Mattson doubts the breadth of significance is as clear for hybrid forms.

Adonis: continuing force versus historical influence. Palm, Sward and Carlberg raise this. I accept it as the key test and say it must be argued from the poems. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg add that translation loss for prosody and sound differs in kind from loss for prose architecture. I and Sem-Sandberg disagree about whether translation uncertainty should itself decide the matter, since that could favour writers who translate most readily.
Tawada: whether the wordplay and conceptual premise carry sufficient weight (Sem-Sandberg, Mattson, Sward) and whether the later novels match the earlier work (Sward, Olsson).
attribution_disputes: No file disputes the identity of any credited writer, and all configurations name exactly one writer. The disagreements are about citation scope within a writer and about differences between proposed laureates.
The proposals differ in laureate: Cărtărescu (B029), Carson (B012), Tawada (B001) and Adonis (B027) are different laureates, not variants of one prize part.

Citation wording differs even for the same laureate. For Carson, Carlberg centres ancient-modern encounter, while Palm names lyric, essay, narrative, translation and the book as object, so the two proposals differ on how translation and design are credited.

For Cărtărescu, Mattson and Sem-Sandberg both anchor the citation in prose with poetry as foundation. Sem-Sandberg leaves open whether poetry is named as a co-equal strand, and Carlberg and Palm note the poetry is thinly covered in translation.

For Carson, Palm would treat translation and scholarship as context for the original writing. Sward also says to rest the citation on original work, and Carlberg says the poems and formal intelligence of the books should carry it, with translations as context. How much weight translations and classical scholarship should carry remains open.

For Tawada, Sward and Mattson agree the citation should name Japanese and German and state the language of each work discussed. They have not settled the balance between fiction and poetry, essays and drama.

For Adonis, my proposal rests on the poetry, with the essays counted only as far as they bear on poetic language. Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg say contested public positions must not count for or against the literary assessment.
maturity_disputes: Adonis: whether the later collections sustain the level of the early and middle work is unresolved. I, Sward and Carlberg say we cannot show it. Timing and age are stated not to be literary criteria.

Cărtărescu: whether Solenoid and the later novels extend the earlier architecture or re-run its obsessions. Sem-Sandberg proposes testing this by reading the texts, and Mattson says it needs close reading by readers of Romanian.

Carson: whether the later work matches Autobiography of Red and Nox. Palm and Carlberg say they have not verified this, and Sem-Sandberg doubts the consistency of the later experiments. Whether a compact corpus can show the sustained depth that a whole-body-of-work prize implies is raised by Palm, Mattson and Carlberg.

Tawada: whether the later novels carry the same formal invention as the earlier work (Sward, Olsson), and whether a partial corpus is being judged because poetry and drama are least visible in translation.
Wider translation of Cărtărescu's work is offered by Sem-Sandberg as a reason reception now matches the work's scale. Mattson replies that wider translation is not evidence of quality.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Carlberg is a co-opted member, and whether co-opted members vote in committee is undocumented. Her simulated vote is a modeling assumption. She records no tie to any shortlisted writer.

I am the chair and my first choice is Adonis. My profile records scholarly interests in modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature. I treat these as context, not as evidence of a preference, and no personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer is recorded. The files disclose this and I do not adjudicate it.

Palm (myth, ekphrasis and women's artistic lives) and Sem-Sandberg (documentary and Central European fiction) each disclose their own literary practice as context. Each states it requires no recusal and treats it as no evidence of preference.
Carlberg and I both flag that contested public and critical positions attributed to Adonis could colour a reading of his work. We agree they must not count for or against the literary assessment.
No member reports a recusal need. Any claim of conflict here is limited to what the six round 1 files state, and I do not verify these disclosures independently.
questions_for_round2: Cărtărescu: Given that Mattson and Sem-Sandberg both leave open whether Solenoid and the later novels deepen or repeat the earlier architecture, what specific passages, volumes or features of structure would each member point to as showing depth or repetition? Should poetry be named in a B029 citation at all, given thin translation coverage?

Adonis: What specific evidence from the poems, rather than from historical influence, supports the continuing force and the quality of the later collections? What would the Academy's regional expert input on Arabic poetry need to establish before members who ranked him sixth or seventh would reassess?

Carson: Should translations and classical scholarship be named in a citation or treated as context for the original writing? What are the core books on which a citation would rest, and how should the committee weigh design-dependent works it cannot judge from the text?

Tawada: How should a citation weigh the Japanese and German bodies of work against each other and fiction against poetry, essays and drama? Can members who cannot read both languages say whether the formal method is sustained in the later novels?

Between B029 and B012, the two ballots with two explicit first-choice supporters each: should whole-oeuvre significance be judged mainly by cumulative architecture or by formal renewal across genres, and does the will's phrase about an idealistic direction favour one reading? Members who rank one of these candidates first and the other second, or who list one as an alternative, are invited to say what would change their order.

Can any member state which of the four first-choice candidates they could support as a laureate if their own first choice does not reach four votes? Answers should rest on the stated criteria, and we should check whether the shared translation uncertainty is being used to separate candidates it does not actually separate.

In my own file I called Cărtărescu my first alternative while the opening ranking lists Carson second and Cărtărescu third. Can I clarify whether these two are close to equal for me, and can others who see tied alternatives say so explicitly?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows four distinct first choices with two supporters each for B029 and B012 and one each for B001 and B027. No configuration approaches the four-vote majority, and no member has stated support for a second candidate as a laureate. The members largely agree on the criteria and on the limits of translation and verification, and the differences are mostly about how to weigh scale, formal renewal, bilingual method and the assessable core of each oeuvre. The files disclose conflicts and uncertainties but do not resolve them. This summary reports only positions explicit in the six round 1 files and does not infer hidden votes.
